Our framework provides a principled characterization of human impressionability and introduces a unified optimization scheme that enables robust and adaptable decision-making across diverse query costs and evaluation objectives without retraining. We evaluate the framework in three HAC settings, examining adaptation to query costs and prediction objectives without retraining, and show that its induced policies perform comparably to or better than the evaluated baselines.

papers.title: Fidelity Collapses with Table Size, Not Turn Count: Delivery Architecture in a Deployed Tool-Using Agent
papers.abstract: When a multi-turn agent delivers a tool's structured records into the model's context and re-emits them each turn, every turn can corrupt data the tool computed correctly. We measure this in a production award-travel agent: two architectures over identical frozen payloads, lineage-matched prompts and sampling, differing only in delivery architecture. SYNTHESIS feeds full record sets into the planner's context and answers follow-ups in-head; BYPASS, the deployed system, keeps records in session state, translates follow-ups into arguments for a deterministic filter, and delivers rows over a typed side channel. Across 24 dialogues (339 scored turns per condition), BYPASS scores 92.3% of turns fully correct, SYNTHESIS 45.7% (paired gap +46.6pp [+35.7, +57.1]). Varying delivered-table size by capture date, SYNTHESIS collapses from near-perfect at 10 rows or fewer to 8% or less beyond about 74 rows. On a content-controlled prefix ladder the collapse threshold orders by model capability, from under 10 rows (GPT-4o-mini) to about 198 or more (Gemini 2.5 Pro), while BYPASS stays size-flat for all four models. The collapse is expensive: beyond 100 rows, where almost no SYNTHESIS answer is correct, each correct one costs roughly 200x BYPASS's flat \$0.012. Practitioners converged on typed side-channel delivery for rendering, not correctness; we show it was, unknowingly, also a correctness decision.

papers.title: Validation of the five-electron pO qubit in Si using full configuration interaction
papers.abstract: The $pO$ qubit is a recently proposed charge qubit consisting of five electrons confined in a gate-defined Si quantum dot. Because its two qubit states have no dipole moment, it couples to electric fields only through the quadrupole moment, suppressing the dominant decoherence channel of conventional charge qubits while retaining all-electrical control. The original proposal was formulated in a shell-filling picture without Coulomb interactions. In this work we perform full configuration interaction (FCI) calculations to assess the impact of the Coulomb interaction on the viability of the $pO$ qubit. We find that the interacting eigenstates occupy orbital shells beyond the shell-filling picture, with the degree of excitation governed by the competition between valley splitting, orbital energy, and Coulomb energy scales. Additionally, we find that the ground states form degenerate doublets, but of two distinct kinds. Above a crossover near a valley splitting of $E_{\rm{VS}}\approx50~μ$eV the doublet is a pair of orbital angular momentum excitations with $|\langle L_z\rangle|=1$ in the lower valley, while below the crossover the doublet is a pair of single valley excitations with $\langle L_z\rangle=0$. Despite this substantial departure from the shell-filling picture, for $E_{\rm{VS}} > 50~μ$eV the essential features, vanishing dipole moments and nonzero quadrupole tensor between qubit states are preserved. We show that the vanishing dipole is in fact guaranteed by the symmetry properties of the five-electron Hamiltonian. The same energy scales that govern the orbital occupation also set the quadrupole tensor elements and the first excited state energy gap, both of which are in principle tunable through device engineering.

papers.title: CLiS: Plug-and-Play Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion on TPUs via Certified Stabilization
papers.abstract: High-resolution video diffusion relies on attention over long token sequences, making attention efficiency critical to generation latency. Our analysis identifies repeated maximum reductions and accumulator rescaling in online softmax as a bottleneck in long-context TPU attention. We propose CLiS (Certified Loop-invariant Stabilization), a training-free, plug-and-play optimization for video diffusion inference. CLiS fixes per-row stabilizers before the KV loop and certifies numerical safety per head, falling back to online softmax when certification fails. It integrates into existing fused-attention kernels without changing model weights or architecture. On Wan 2.2 and LTX-2 across TPU v6e and TPU7x, CLiS reduces diffusion transformer (DiT) step latency by up to 19.6% relative to tuned online softmax without measurable quality loss. Controlled TPU adaptations of prior GPU stabilization methods show performance or numerical-safety limitations. Preliminary causal LLM experiments also show up to 13.5% higher training throughput in continued pretraining and 7.7% in supervised fine-tuning.

papers.title: Multivariate analogues of Ruijsenaars' hypergeometric function
papers.abstract: We construct multivariate analogues of Ruijsenaars' hypergeometric function as nested products of overlap coefficients between eigenfunctions of twisted primitive elements in representations of the modular double of $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. The construction is a hyperbolic counterpart of the nested multivariate Askey--Wilson polynomials and functions. Using iterated coproducts, we derive four systems of difference equations for which these multivariate functions are joint eigenfunctions. The four systems correspond to the two sets of variables and the two step sizes $iw_1$ and $iw_2$, which are interchanged by modular duality. We also prove that Ruijsenaars' one-variable transform is unitary in the parameter regime required for the construction, for positive as well as complex conjugate $w_1,w_2$. A two-sided normalization of the kernel separates the input and output weights, so that iterating one-variable transforms yields unitary multivariate transforms with explicit inverse and Plancherel formulas.

papers.title: Analog and hybrid computing in the 21st century
papers.abstract: Analog computers solve problems through physical representations of mathematical variables and relations, often using the dynamics of electronic circuits and their associated signals. Many analog computers directly represent nonlinear dynamical systems; they encode their solutions in the signals that they generate. Although most modern scientific computing relies on digital architectures with inherently discrete-valued representations and algorithmic approaches, the design constraints of such architectures increasingly limit both performance and energy efficiency. Analog systems can circumvent some of these constraints; they execute specific computations very efficiently by mapping them directly onto physical processes using smaller and simpler computing elements than the ones in digital architectures. In this article, we provide an interdisciplinary perspective on modern analog and hybrid (i.e., analog-digital) computing. We discuss how modern scientific computing workflows can leverage analog approaches in various applications, such as in simulating dynamical systems, performing optimization, and enabling more energy-efficient implementations of artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Quantiles, Not Points: Streaming Quantile Matching for Ordinal-Aware LLM-as-a-Judge Calibration
papers.abstract: LLM-as-a-judge scores are often distributionally shifted from human ratings on any given evaluation task, and post-hoc calibration (mapping LLM to human scores in a small labeled anchor set) has become a popular method to correct for this shift. In this paper we derive the calibration from two positions: that LLMaJ scores are ordinal ratings drawn from a distribution rather than isolated points. We present streaming quantile matching (SQM), a version of a classical method not previously bench marked for LLMaJ calibration, which is built on the two positions by computing the optimal-transport map between the LLM and human score distributions. We develop an evaluation framework and within it we show that unlike point-wise calibrations, SQM respects the ordinality of the human anchor set and achieves the best distributional fidelity and the top overall rank across models and data. We also show that in general, post-hoc calibration narrows the raw error gap between smaller and larger judge models, which opens the possibility of more efficient LLM judges.

papers.title: Learning to evolve by matching velocities
papers.abstract: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.

papers.title: SpBench: An Agent-Native Framework for Cross-Engine Lakehouse Benchmarking
papers.abstract: SpBench is an agent-native framework for cross-engine lakehouse benchmarking, in production use for benchmarking Snowpark, Snowpark Connect for Apache Spark, and other execution environments across standardized suites -- such as TPCx-BB and TPC-DI -- and custom benchmarks distilled from production workload patterns. It runs continuously across a broad portfolio of workloads, guiding the performance roadmap and detecting regressions for production-scale data engines. Benchmarking has historically been an expensive investment requiring continuous cross-functional collaboration and domain expertise, making it difficult to obtain actionable performance insights. SpBench provides (i) a typed, code-generated benchmark substrate that compiles platform-agnostic benchmark definitions into fair, comparable platform-specific implementations; (ii) a structured-telemetry contract recording every run as queryable fact and dimension data, letting LLM agents query results deterministically; and (iii) an agent-native harness of three composable skills to expedite building benchmarks and analyzing results. This agent-native architecture enabled the rapid development of more than 400 benchmark queries that run on a regular cadence to detect performance regressions; catching these has directly led to improvements in production.

papers.title: From Lookups to Lessons: Turning Retrieved Knowledge into Parametric Memory
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) helps large language models (LLMs) answer factual questions beyond their training data, but it adds storage and inference costs. Distilling previously retrieved information into parametric memories enables reuse without online retrieval. However, training the memory to mimic a retriever rewards accurate independent predictions, which do not necessarily improve the final output quality when combined with the LLM's existing predictions. To address this, we introduce ResMem, in which the LLM reads retrieved text offline to generate teacher targets. This design avoids storing massive token representations, unlike existing parametric memory approaches such as MLP Memory, which relies on k-nearest neighbor (kNN) datastores. Furthermore, by using the LLM as an offline teacher that reads privileged retrieved evidence alongside the input, we train a parametric memory to learn an additive logit residual. This residual aligns the predictions of a student sharing the same backbone with the teacher distribution, while self-distillation updates remain confined to the parametric memory. On a Wikipedia subset, ResMem reduces the storage retained for teacher construction by 94.7% compared with the evaluated kNN pipeline. Across five question answering datasets, ResMem raises mean token F1 from 32.83% for the frozen LLM to 34.48%. It also breaks 21% fewer of the LLM's correct answers than a kNN-trained memory. These findings validate our motivation of treating retrieval as a learning resource, with parametric memory shaped by how retrieved knowledge is used to inform the model's future predictions. Code and model weights are available at https://github.com/SSRand/From-Lookups-to-Lessons and https://huggingface.co/RandHan/ResMem-Mistral-7B-v0.3.

papers.title: Order continuity of induced homomorphisms between free Banach lattices
papers.abstract: Let $T\colon F\to E$ be a bounded operator between Banach spaces and let $\overline T\colon FBL^{(p)}[F]\to FBL^{(p)}[E]$ be the lattice homomorphism induced by $T$ between the corresponding free $p$-convex Banach lattices generated by $F$ and $E$. We show that $\overline T$ is order continuous if and only if it is either zero or a lattice isomorphic embedding. For $p=\infty$, this holds precisely when $T$ is zero or an isomorphic embedding, while for $1\leq p<\infty$, apart from the zero operator, $T$ must be an embedding and the pair $(T(F),E)$ must have the operator-extension property POE-$p$. In addition, we study when $FBL^{(p)}[E]$ is order dense or majorizing in $FBL^{(q)}[E]$ for $p<q$.

papers.title: Compositional Self-Improvement: Promises and Pitfalls
papers.abstract: Although self-improvement is becoming increasingly important as tasks become more complex, models struggle to generate reliable supervision for harder, out-of-distribution instances. One way to address this challenge is to exploit compositional structure: models often solve simpler subproblems more reliably than full problems, so their subproblem predictions can be composed into supervision for harder ones. We systematically study when this kind of composed supervision supports self-improvement and when it fails. Our controlled experiments identify three failure modes: unreliable subproblem predictions, errors introduced by composition, and limited supervision coverage. Beyond controlled settings, these findings carry over to more realistic coding and reasoning tasks: composed labels are more accurate than direct self-generated labels and improve performance even on compositions longer than those seen during training, while the failure modes remain visible. Further, although these failure modes often keep compositional self-improvement from fully succeeding on its own, a short SFT warmup with compositional self-improvement can bootstrap reinforcement learning on tasks that require composing skills the model already has, particularly when direct exploration rarely succeeds. Together, these findings characterize when compositional self-improvement can provide sufficiently reliable supervision to expand model capabilities.

papers.title: mmWave UE Positioning Under Blockage: Limits for ISAC-Assisted Handover
papers.abstract: Proactive handover can save a millimeter-wave (mmWave) link before a passing body blocks it, but only if the network knows where the user is. We ask whether the radio units that serve a user can localize it accurately enough from its uplink sounding reference signals. We derive position error bounds that include synchronization and array calibration errors, with and without reflected paths known from a digital twin, and test two estimators in a ray-traced street canyon on held-out scenarios. Three findings stand out. First, with line of sight to both radio units, array calibration, not bandwidth, limits the bound. Second, blockage degrades the line-of-sight-only bound sharply, whereas known reflections keep the map-aided bound low. Third, a simple dominant-path estimator fails where it matters most: its errors grow sharply around blockage, and proactive handover becomes worse than the 3GPP baseline. A map-aided multipath tracker cuts the median error from 12 to 3.7 cm and removes this significant penalty at link margins of 15 dB and above, but does not yet beat the baseline.

papers.title: Bilinear Strichartz Estimates and Linear Morawetz Estimates for Schrödinger Operators with Potentials
papers.abstract: In dimensions three and above, we establish bilinear Strichartz estimates for Schrödinger operators with potentials using perturbative arguments and Morawetz estimates. Our approach does not require smallness of the potential. As part of the analysis, we also establish endpoint versions of the bilinear Christ-Kiselev lemma.

papers.title: TacMind: Benchmarking and Modeling Tactile Interaction States for Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct observations of contact physics, local geometry, and interaction dynamics, making it a vital source of feedback for contact-rich manipulation. However, existing tactile manipulation studies are often developed and evaluated within specific task settings, making it difficult to systematically compare how tactile information contributes under different interaction conditions. In this work, we develop a benchmark in simulation comprising 128 tasks organized around three complementary evaluation regimes: Precise, Recognition, and Dynamic. The benchmark further includes controlled static and dynamic task variants and 12 perturbation settings for evaluating robustness under changes in visual and physical conditions. These settings motivate studying tactile information as a temporally evolving interaction representation rather than only as an instantaneous observation. We therefore propose an action-conditioned latent predictive world model that integrates tactile history and learns a tactile state through prediction of future tactile latents. Building on this representation, we design a model that conditions action generation on the learned tactile state and uses predicted future tactile information to refine candidate actions through predictive tactile reflection. Experiments on the proposed benchmark show consistent gains from incorporating tactile information across the evaluated regimes. Project Page: https://tacmind-bench.github.io/

papers.title: Spectral Fields and Unitary Descent: Local splitting, simultaneous norms, and transcendental obstructions
papers.abstract: Spectral fields can recover matrix coefficients without standardizing the invariant Hermitian form. Over an algebraic subfield of $\mathbb{C}$ stable under nontrivial complex conjugation, we prove that every Zariski-dense subgroup in a normalized Hermitian model of dimension $m\ge4$ and signature $(m-1,1)$ at the fixed embedding contains a loxodromic element whose spectrum makes all diagonal coefficients norms. The element can be chosen so that every positive power is regular and generates the same splitting field. For an arbitrary initial Hermitian model over such a field, two spectra suffice for standard unitary descent over an extension of relative degree at most $(m!)^2$. Over every quadratic extension $F/k$ of nonarchimedean local fields of characteristic zero, a four-dimensional quasi-split unitary group of Witt index two contains a discrete, Zariski-dense free subgroup whose spectra all split over $F$. Over intrinsic fields of positive transcendence degree, we construct a single convex cocompact, Zariski-dense free subgroup of $\mathrm{SU}(3,1)$ for which, for every initial regular element and every normalized extraction, the Hermitian obstruction persists after adjoining any finite family of spectra and over the total spectral field.

papers.title: Bilateral Christoffel-Geronimus-Uvarov formulas for mixed-type orthogonality on algebraic supports
papers.abstract: Christoffel-type determinant formulas construct both normalized polynomial families and their reproducing kernel for mixed-type orthogonality in several variables after independent rational matrix transformations on the two arguments. The pairing may have a rectangular matrix of functionals, with separate degree bounds on each component, and may be supported on an algebraic variety. The reduced matrices are calculated from the original biorthogonal polynomials, rational moments, polynomial division and the masses left free by division; their nonvanishing determinants characterize existence and uniqueness. For measure pairings the rational data are expressed by Cauchy and multivariate Fantappie transforms. Exact dimension counts incorporate the four matrix factors and the relations of the support. For normal degree-ordered original families and fixed factors, when the component degrees on each side differ by a bounded amount and the normalization dimension grows at most like one degree layer, the resulting orders are bounded on curves and grow at most linearly on surfaces. For pairings allowing scalar factors to move between arguments, called balanced pairings, an exact obstruction determines whether a bilateral mass decomposes into unilateral masses when the denominators act injectively. Residue duality provides coordinates for division and mass quotients on integral curves, including singular points, and on the finite surface quotients specified here. Explicit singular-curve families retain nondegenerate residue pairings as denominator zeros coalesce. Positive congruences admit a further reduction by orthogonal projection, while balanced pairings give simultaneous intertwining identities for all coordinate multiplication matrices.

papers.title: PRISM-Net: Dynamic Routing Network with VLM-Guided Disentangled Attribute Distillation for Explainable Fine-Grained Product Retrieval
papers.abstract: Fine-grained visual product retrieval in large-scale e-commerce multimedia systems demands discriminative representations capable of simultaneously resolving macro-level category semantics and micro-level visual attributes such as structural contour (line) and chromatic appearance (color). However, conventional backbones including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and vision Transformers (ViTs) inherently suffer from feature entanglement and shortcut learning. To learn the micro-level visual attributes without costly manual attribute annotations, we propose phase-routed interpretable semantic mixture-of-experts network (PRISM-Net), an explainable multi-expert architecture that disentangles holistic visual features into disentangled line and color expert pathways governed by a conditional meta-router. In phase 1, we introduce an external VLM-Guided sigmoid semantic distillation mechanism with gradient-detached routing gates, utilizing zero-shot text prompts from SigLIP to supervise specialized structural and chromatic experts. In phase 2, the disentangled expert embeddings are adaptively fused with macro base features via a learned meta-router gate to calibrate category boundaries. Extensive 5-fold cross-validation across 275,454 e-commerce images (18 categories) and full-scale retrieval benchmarks (55,091 queries against a 220,363-image gallery) across SwinV2, ConvNeXt-V2, and DINOv3 demonstrate substantial gains. On SwinV2, PRISM-Net boosts full-fold product mAP@10 from 80.98% to 83.90% (+2.92%), line mAP@10 by +5.74%, and color mAP@10 by +9.12%. Furthermore, unsupervised distribution analysis of the meta-router gate reveals that both ViT and CNN backbones emergently allocate up to 6.8x higher structural line weights to rigid appliances and hardware while dedicating >96% chromatic weight to clothing.

papers.title: Clarkson--McCarthy type inequalities, part II: refinements, unitary orbits, unitarily invariant norms and $\ell_s$--$\ell_s$ estimates
papers.abstract: In previous work \cite{Zha26a}, the author established Clarkson--McCarthy type inequalities for several classes of operator families, including $\ell_p$--$\ell_p$ estimates and mixed $\ell_q$--$\ell_p$ estimates, by means of operator square-sum identities. The present paper has two main aims. First, using the tracial joint spectral measures recently introduced by O.~Heinävaara \cite{Hei25}, we obtain several refinements of the McCarthy--Clarkson inequalities, one of which confirms a conjecture of Audenaert \cite{AK17}. Second, combining tools from matrix analysis with complex interpolation theory, we establish Clarkson--McCarthy type inequalities for unitary orbits, unitarily invariant norms, and $\ell_s$--$\ell_s$ estimates, again in the framework of operator square-sum identities.

papers.title: From Small to Large: Assessing Medical Reasoning, Benchmark Contamination, and Model Size in Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now answer medical exam questions at or above expert level, but it is unclear whether such scores reflect clinical competence, or are instead affected by the format of the questions being asked (e.g., multiple-choice versus open-ended), prior exposure to the benchmarks, and the difficulty of the questions. These benchmarks are also public and widely used online, which may be resulting in LLM memorization. Models may perform better on questions that they have seen before. It is also not evident whether smaller models, which are more locally deployable in HIPAA-compliant hospital settings, have achieved human performance. In this study, we evaluate fourteen current models from six leading providers, one smaller and one larger model from each provider with two additional open-weight models, on 3,076 questions from four medical benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and MedBullets) under standard multiple choice, the same questions with the answer choices withheld, and reconstruction of a hidden question from its choices alone. In the standard multiple-choice setting, the strongest models exceed the human-expert baseline on MedQA-USMLE and PubMedQA, but the smaller models trail their larger models by 8.7 percentage points and only two of the six pass the human-expert bar on the licensing examination. Withholding the answer choices, however, makes every model struggle: mean accuracy falls from 82.3% to 50.9%, and the two largest drops belong to the medically specialised models. On memorization, the strongest models reconstruct one question in four from the answer choices alone, yet accuracy holds on the questions they cannot reconstruct. We further weigh accuracy against inference cost and test whether ensembling several models improves medical question answering.

papers.title: $k$-Center under Weak and Strong Distance Oracles with an Application to Minimum Sum of Radii Clustering
papers.abstract: In the weak-strong distance oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram and Wang (COLT 2024), a metric $(X,d)$ on $n$ points is accessed through two oracles: a cheap weak oracle that returns each queried distance correctly with probability $1-δ$ and permits arbitrary values on corrupted pairs, chosen by an adversary who knows the entire metric and all corrupted pairs, and an expensive strong oracle that reveals a point exactly. The goal is to cluster well while making as few strong queries as possible. Our main result is a $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $k$-center using $O(k\log n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ strong point queries, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$. This improves both the $(14+\varepsilon)$ approximation factor and the $O(k\log^2 n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ query bound of Bateni et al. It also improves the query complexity of the recent $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Pradhan, Bhattacharya and Jaiswal (AISTATS 2026), in the variant of the model they study. Our algorithm outputs an explicitly known sketch of an otherwise unknown metric: a concrete metric on at most $k$ points that a downstream algorithm can compute with directly, with no further queries and no noise. As an application, we give a simple FPT algorithm for Minimum Sum of Radii (MSR) that returns a constant-factor solution using $2^{O(k\log k)}\cdot O(\log n\log\log n)$ strong queries. We complement the upper bound with an $Ω(k\log(n/k))$ lower bound for $k$-center with assignment that holds for row-local algorithms. These algorithms assign two unqueried points to the same center whenever their weak distances to the strong-queried points are exactly the same. Our algorithm and those of Bateni et al. and Pradhan et al. are all row-local, so our query bound is optimal for this class up to the $O(\log\log n)$ factor.

papers.title: Siting and Curtailment Depth Limit the Grid Headroom Available to New Large Loads
papers.abstract: Data center demand is increasing faster than generation can be built, encouraging proposals to interconnect large loads on condition that they reduce consumption during high-stress periods. Estimates of how much load can be added via flexibility rest on simplified accounting and report only annual curtailed electricity. Here we use a national energy systems model that co-optimizes hourly generation and load curtailment across 16 U.S. regions to characterize the flexibility and power system impacts of enabling headroom. While 50 GW can be served while curtailing less than 0.1% of its annual energy, small annual curtailment conceals potentially severe operating requirements. Most regions require curtailment deeper than 90% in at least one hour, so the load must disconnect or have sufficient on-site resources to provide full back up. Furthermore, announced data center locations are not aligned with modeled headroom and relying on existing generation fleets raises CO2 emissions and wholesale electricity prices.

papers.title: Exo: An Architecture for Self-Improving Systems at Runtime
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses govern how language models act in an environment; designing their policies by hand is difficult, while automated techniques require representative datasets and costly executions. We present Exo, an agent runtime architecture for safe learning during ongoing work that collapses the optimization loop into task execution, allowing agents to revise both their harness and their strategies for further improvement. A minimal protected mechanism layer preserves execution history and governs policy activation while the harness evolves through inspectable code changes. On long-running objectives in an open-world game, Exo reduces model cost by 12-53% relative to Codex and Pi in standalone runs and 45-82% in transfer runs, while matching task completion rates. Compared with the same starting policy without the ability to edit policy, Exo reduces held-out model cost by 35-61% on AppWorld and SREGym with comparable correctness, cutting AppWorld's mean task time by 13% and SREGym's median diagnosis time by 35%. On Continual Learning Bench coding tasks, model cost including learning falls by 14%, with both policies resolving every issue.

papers.title: Compression Technique Interactions in Small Language Models: A Factorial Ablation Study
papers.abstract: Deploying small language models on resource-constrained hardware requires compression, yet practitioners lack systematic guidance on how quantization, pruning, and post-compression recovery interact when combined. We present a factorial ablation study evaluating 72 compression configurations across four SLM architectures (2.7B-7B parameters), extended with a 48-configuration ordering analysis, benchmark accuracy validation on 30 compressed models, and robustness checks including multi-seed validation and full-corpus perplexity evaluation. INT8 quantization is effectively lossless (<0.5% accuracy degradation), while NF4 quantization combined with L1 magnitude pruning causes model collapse in all 16 tested combinations. LoRA-based fine-tuning reduces degraded perplexity by up to 97% after aggressive pruning; an ablation against standard fine-tuning without a teacher model shows the recovery is driven by LoRA adaptation itself rather than the distillation signal. Compression ordering shows no significant effect among viable configurations (ANOVA p = 0.96) but determines viability for NF4+pruning combinations. INT8 quantization alone provides 40-45% memory reduction with no quality loss. On-device CPU deployment via llama.cpp confirms these findings transfer off the GPU: 4-bit quantization runs 46-54% faster than 8-bit for a perplexity difference under 0.5 points, while un-structured pruning yields no CPU latency or memory benefit, consistent with its dense storage format.

papers.title: The Promises and Limitations of Evaluation-Based AI Governance: Evidence from Expert Interviews
papers.abstract: We conducted 37 semi-structured expert interviews to examine how frontier AI evaluations reduce societal-level AI risks. Evaluations have become central to AI risk governance, despite their shortcomings being widely critiqued. Still, the case for how they reduce risks in practice remains largely implicit. Drawing on expert accounts, we reconstruct this case by identifying the mechanisms through which evaluations are expected to reduce risk, the assumptions underpinning those mechanisms, and the challenges those assumptions face. Our findings suggest that `evaluation-based governance' could contain foundational gaps which undermine risk-reduction strategies that depend on evaluations. Using thematic analysis, we identified three key pathways through which evaluations could reduce risk: by (i) making societal-level risks concrete to decision-makers and the public (raised in 18 out of 37 interviews), (ii) serving as a basis for governance commitments and regulation (18), and (iii) incentivizing a better risk culture within AI companies (16). However, these pathways often depended on shared assumptions that participants themselves doubted. The main challenges included, in order of frequency: (i) diminishing informativeness of evaluation results as model capabilities improve (21), (ii) measurement limitations that may be inherent to the evaluation paradigm (18), (iii) a lack of guarantees that evaluation results will be acted upon by companies or governments (16), and (iv) the degree of control and discretion AI companies retain over evaluation design, disclosure, and response (12). Participants also noted that evaluation-based governance could prove counterproductive, by functioning as a permission structure for developers' continued capability improvement (4). We finish by discussing the implications of our findings for evaluation-based governance, and what would improve its prospects.

papers.title: Security and Derivative Pricing with Fast Regime Switches
papers.abstract: A regime-switching model lets any parameter of a standard model take a different value in each state of a hidden Markov chain. For the affine and exponential-Lévy models in common use the pricing problem reduces to one linear system, a' = (Q + diag g(t)) a, with the chain's generator Q and a model-specific forcing g as its only ingredients. We expand its solution in the mean holding time of the chain to any order, with an initial layer for the starting regime, and identify the first correction as a Green-Kubo matrix from the group inverse of Q. The same system prices bonds, swaptions, caps, credit default swaps, Asian and digital options, and equity options under stochastic rates, with the Gil-Pelaez integrals conditioned on the regime at expiry where a payoff depends on it; barrier, American and Bermudan instruments go to the coupled equations on a grid. Every numerical claim is checked against QuantLib in the limit where the regimes coincide and against an independent referee with switching on, and the implementation is public.

papers.title: Penalized Likelihood Inference in Highly Multivariate Sparse Spectral Graphical Gaussian Processes
papers.abstract: We develop a penalized likelihood inference approach for highly multivariate Gaussian stochastic processes. Since zeros in the inverse cross-spectral density encode process-level conditional independence, sparse modeling of this object provides a natural route to scalable inference in the highly multivariate case. We introduce a latent variable representation which, combined with random Fourier features, yields a stochastic approximation expectation--maximization algorithm for penalized maximum likelihood estimation of a sparse inverse cross-spectral density matrix under a graphical LASSO penalty. The augmentation is crucial because sparsity is present in the inverse spectral density of the latent variable, whereas the marginal inverse covariance remains dense in the presence of a spatial nugget. Our frequency domain formulation enables joint penalized likelihood estimation of process-specific spatial covariance parameters and sparse process-level conditional dependence without requiring a pre-specified reference set of locations. The method is demonstrated on both synthetic and the MERRA-2 aerosol reanalysis data sets, yielding benefit over existing alternatives, especially for prediction at unobserved locations under spatial misalignment.

papers.title: The symbolic pfaffian method I: A generalization of the Gallucio-Loebl-Tesler Theorem
papers.abstract: The pfaffian number of a graph $G$, denoted by $\mathrm{pf}(G)$, is the minimum integer $k$ such that the generating function of perfect matchings of $G$ can be written as a linear combination of $k$ pfaffians of signed adjacency matrices. The Galluccio-Loebl-Tesler Theorem states that $\mathrm{pf}(G) \leq 4^g$, where $g$ is the orientable genus of $G$. We generalize this theorem by relating the pfaffian number of a graph to another graph parameter: the symbolic pfaffian number, denoted by $\mathrm{spf}(G)$. Namely, we prove that $\mathrm{pf}(G) \leq 2^{\mathrm{spf}(G)}$. Our proof is based on linear algebra arguments and does not depend on topological properties of graphs. As a consequence of our generalization, we conclude that $\mathrm{pf}(K_{2n}) = 2^{\mathcal{O}(n \log n)}$, an improvement on the previous upper bound of $4^{\mathcal{O}(n^2)}$ based on the genus. We also consider lower bounds for $\mathrm{pf}(G)$ related to $\mathrm{spf}(G)$. In particular, we show that the graphs with $\mathrm{pf}(G) = 4$ are the graphs with $\mathrm{spf}(G) = 2$. On the other hand, we show that our main result is strictly more general than a previous generalization by Norine.

papers.title: Steering Readerly Dynamics: Trajectory-Guided Story Generation with Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate stories, but these stories struggle to reproduce engaging readerly dynamics, the evolving reader responses that shape narrative experience. To address this challenge, we propose a framework that learns readerly dynamics from high-quality human-written stories and uses them to guide story generation. Instead of directly modeling high-dimensional story content, we train a small LLM to predict future reader responses as low-dimensional trajectories. We then leverage the strong instruction-following capability of a larger, off-the-shelf writer LLM to generate story segments that follow these predicted trajectories within a given story setting. Our framework improves trajectory-based fidelity to human-written stories by 12%-35% while largely preserving story coherence.

papers.title: Guide to Teaching with Data in Statistics and Data Science Classrooms
papers.abstract: Statistics and data science educators have been concerned about data use or lack thereof in the classroom for decades. For many educators, the question is not whether to use data or not. They often want to know whether they should give clean or messy data, and whether they should spend the time to find a real dataset or simulate it. If they decide to find real data, then other questions follow about where to find it and how to provide it to students. If they provide data, then the question remains whether students will find the data engaging or not or if it will have the properties necessary to demonstrate class concepts. We provide empirically and theoretically supported recommendations on data use. Classroom data are described in different ways (e.g., real, raw, made-up, artificial, fictitious, synthetic, simulated, toy, and messy). We provide definitions of different types, sources, formats, and shapes of data and provide distinctions between classifications. We share resources for educators in bringing data to their classrooms.

papers.title: Mutual Information Estimation via Triangular Transport Maps: Finite Sample Guarantees and Sample Allocation
papers.abstract: We study finite sample guarantees for transport based mutual information estimation. Mutual information can be estimated by first learning the conditional and marginal densities and then evaluating their log-density ratio by Monte Carlo. Given training samples, we use triangular transport maps to learn these densities and then compute the mutual information estimate on an independent batch of evaluation samples. For conditional density estimation using triangular transport maps, we establish non-asymptotic guarantees over realizable Hölder classes by viewing the conditional density as an ordinary density with respect to the product of the law of the conditioning variable and Lebesgue measure. This allows standard density estimation techniques to be applied directly to the conditional density estimation. These results yield finite sample guarantees for the resulting mutual information estimator and characterize how a fixed sample budget should be allocated between training and evaluation in order to minimize the mean squared error. Numerical experiments support the predicted training and evaluation error rates and illustrate the resulting sample allocation tradeoff.

papers.title: FESTiVE: Self-calibrated Spatial-temporal Gradient Characterization for Non-cartesian Imaging on High Performance Systems
papers.abstract: Gradient imperfections disrupt the encoding benefits of long-readout imaging applications on high-performance systems. Currently, external field monitoring hardware provides the only reliable solution for general spatial-temporal gradient characterization. We present FESTiVE, a data-driven alternative to higher-order field monitoring. FESTiVE leverages parallel imaging to both implicitly model and explicitly recover field imperfections. Using a fast k-t mapping calibration scan, FESTiVE formulates a time-varying GRAPPA problem which maps k-space data corrupted by a time-varying gradient imperfection against a clean reference. This mapping is represented compactly with an implicit neural representation, from which the spatial-temporal fields are recovered in image space using coil sensitivities. In phantom, FESTiVE produces comparable field measurements to a Skope field camera across multiple non-cartesian 2D acquisition strategies and gradient specifications. In vivo, FESTiVE achieves state-of-the-art image quality for a high-performance diffusion spiral protocol on the head-only MAGNUS 3T, where higher-order phase imperfections are significant. At 7T, on the head-only Siemens TerraX system, FESTiVE enables 300μm spiral imaging where conventional field camera-based approaches fall below probe dephasing limits. In conclusion, FESTiVE enables robust high-resolution non-cartesian imaging on high-performance gradients, characterizing gradient imperfections using parallel imaging rather than field monitoring hardware.

papers.title: Stochastic learning flow: moment equations for stochastic gradient descent at finite step size
papers.abstract: Analytical theories of learning in deep networks often assume gradient flow, discarding the finite step size and batch noise of stochastic gradient descent (SGD). Starting from the discrete update, we derive continuous-time equations for the mean and covariance of the parameter distribution under a Gaussian closure for a general stochastic learning, to first order in the learning rate $η$. Applying these stochastic learning flow (SLF) equations to SGD, we show that the mean descends an effective loss regularized by the covariance and loss curvature, while the covariance, unlike in stochastic differential equation approximations, becomes unstable at curvature $2/η$. In SGD ensembles of linear and nonlinear networks, SLF predicts learning curves and mean trajectories more accurately than gradient flow and captures the covariance dynamics, failing where the parameter distribution becomes strongly non-Gaussian. In the full-batch limit, the edge of stability corresponds to a stationary point of the coupled sharpness-covariance dynamics, recovering self-stabilization and central flow, and batch-to-batch curvature fluctuations lower this threshold under SGD.
